name: Reliable sources and honest use
intro: How to evaluate and check sources, misinformation and disinformation, using AI critically, and how to quote, paraphrase and make a source list while respecting privacy and copyright.
sammendrag:
## Why check your sources?

The internet gives us more information than ever – but not all of it is reliable. Some sources contain mistakes, some are one-sided, and some spread **misinformation** (false information, often shared by people who believe it) or **disinformation** (false information spread on purpose). When you write or present in English, you must use sources **critically** and **honestly**.

## Evaluating a source

Ask these questions:

- **Who** made it? Is the author or organisation an expert? Is it a known newspaper, a university, a government site – or an anonymous blog?
- **Why** was it made? To inform, to sell, to entertain or to persuade?
- **When** was it published or updated? Is it still up to date?
- **What** evidence does it give? Are there facts, references and links?
- **Does it agree** with other reliable sources?

Websites of governments, universities and well-known news organisations are often reliable, but you should always think for yourself. **Wikipedia** can be a good starting point, but check the references at the bottom of the article.

## Checking facts

- **Lateral reading**: Instead of staying on one website, open new tabs and see what other sources say about the topic and the sender.
- A **reverse image search** can reveal whether a picture is old, edited or taken out of context.
- **Fact-checking websites** examine viral claims.
- Be extra careful with content that makes you very angry or excited – it may be designed to go viral.

## AI and sources

AI chatbots can help with ideas and explanations, but they can **make things up** and even invent sources that do not exist. Always check important facts in reliable sources, and follow your school's rules for using AI.

## Using sources honestly

- **Quote**: use the exact words in quotation marks and name the source.
- **Paraphrase**: explain the idea in your own words – and still name the source.
- Make a **source list** (bibliography) with the author, title, website or publisher, publication date and the date you read it.

Using someone's words or ideas without giving credit is **plagiarism**.

## Privacy and copyright

When you use sources and create content, you must follow the rules for **privacy** and **copyright**. Don't publish personal information or pictures of others without consent, and only use pictures, music and videos you are allowed to use, such as your own or those with a **Creative Commons** licence.

flashcards.def: A source you can trust because of its expertise, evidence and purpose.
False information, often shared by people who believe it is true.
False information spread on purpose to deceive.
The person or organisation behind a source.
Recent enough to still be correct.
Facts, data and references that support a claim.
Opening new tabs to see what other sources say about a topic and sender.
Searching with a picture to find where else it has been published.
Examining whether a claim is true.

Exact words from a source in quotation marks.
Explaining an idea from a source in your own words.
A list of the sources you have used.
Using someone's words or ideas without giving credit.

Opening new tabs to see what other sources say about a topic and sender
Reading a text from right to left

quiz.text: What can a reverse image search reveal?
options: Whether a picture is old, edited or taken out of context
quiz.explain: Old pictures are often reused in fake news.

options: Explaining an idea in your own words
quiz.explain: You must still name the source when you paraphrase.

quiz.text: What should you remember about AI chatbots?
options: They never make mistakes about sources
They should replace all other sources
They can make things up and invent sources
quiz.explain: Always check important facts in reliable sources.

quiz.text: Why should you check when a source was published?
options: To make sure the information is still up to date
Because dates are required by law
quiz.explain: Facts like statistics can change over time.

options: As a starting point, and check the references
quiz.explain: Anyone can edit Wikipedia, so check where the information comes from.

quiz.text: What should a source list include?
options: Author, title, website or publisher and dates
quiz.explain: The reader should be able to find the source.

quiz.text: Why should you be careful with content that makes you very angry?
options: Because anger is bad for you
Because it may be designed to go viral
quiz.explain: Strong emotions make people share without checking.

quiz.text: What must you do when you quote someone's exact words?
options: Use quotation marks and name the source
quiz.explain: This shows clearly which words are not your own.

ekstra.text: All information on the internet is reliable.
ekstra.explain: Anyone can publish online, so you must evaluate sources.

ekstra.text: Paraphrasing without naming the source can be plagiarism.
ekstra.explain: The idea still belongs to someone else.

ekstra.text: A good source often gives evidence and references.
ekstra.explain: References let you check where the information comes from.

ekstra.text: You can publish pictures of other people without asking them.
ekstra.explain: You need consent to publish pictures of others.

options: False information, often shared by people who believe it
ekstra.explain: Misinformation is not necessarily spread on purpose.

ekstra.text: Which question helps you evaluate a source?
options: How many pictures does it have?
ekstra.explain: The sender and purpose tell you a lot about reliability.

ekstra.text: Which of these can you usually use in your project?
options: Any song from a streaming service
A photo from a stranger's profile
A picture with a Creative Commons licence, following the terms
A clip from a new cinema film
ekstra.explain: Creative Commons licences give permission on certain conditions.

skriv.text: Explain in your own words what makes a source reliable.
skriv.fasit: A reliable source is one you can trust because the sender has relevant expertise, the source gives evidence, and its purpose is trustworthy.
kriterier: Explains that a reliable source can be trusted.
Mentions relevant expertise, evidence and/or purpose as reasons for trust.

skriv.text: A university website gives evidence and names its experts. An anonymous blog makes the same claim but gives no evidence. Compare how reliable the two sources seem and explain why.
skriv.fasit: The university website seems more reliable because it identifies experts and gives evidence. The anonymous blog is harder to trust because its sender is unknown and it gives no evidence.
kriterier: Says the university website seems more reliable, without claiming it must always be correct.
Uses the difference in expertise, sender or evidence to explain the comparison.

skriv.text: A website is trying to sell a product and makes a claim about it. Explain why the website’s purpose matters and what you should check before using the claim.
skriv.fasit: The website may present the claim to persuade people to buy the product. I should check what evidence it gives and compare the claim with other reliable sources.
kriterier: Recognises that the purpose is to sell or persuade, which may affect how the claim is presented.
Says to check evidence and/or compare with other reliable sources.

skriv.text: Two reliable sources disagree about a claim you want to use in a presentation. Explain how you should decide what to include.
skriv.fasit: I should compare the evidence each source gives and check what other reliable sources say. I should not choose a claim just because it appears in one source.
kriterier: Says to examine or compare the evidence behind the claims.
Says to check other reliable sources before deciding what to include.

skriv.text: A claim is spreading online, but you are not sure whether it is true. Explain how a fact-checking website could help you.
skriv.fasit: A fact-checking website examines whether a claim is true. It can help me check the claim before I share or use it.
kriterier: Explains that fact-checking examines whether a claim is true.
Connects this check to deciding whether to use or share the claim.

skriv.text: You explain an idea from a website in your own words, but you do not name the website. Explain what is wrong and how to make your work honest.
skriv.fasit: This is plagiarism because I used someone else’s idea without giving credit. I should name the source even when I explain the idea in my own words.
kriterier: Identifies using an idea without credit as plagiarism.
Says to name or credit the source, even when using your own words.

skriv.text: You want to post a picture of a friend online, but your friend has not agreed to it. What should you do, and why?
skriv.fasit: I should not post the picture without my friend’s consent. This respects their privacy.
kriterier: Says not to publish the picture without consent.

skriv.text: You find a picture online and want to use it in a school presentation. Explain what you need to check and give one kind of picture you are allowed to use.
skriv.fasit: I need to check that I am allowed to use the picture. I can use my own picture or one with a Creative Commons licence, following its conditions.
kriterier: Says to check that the picture is allowed to be used.
Gives an acceptable example, such as their own picture or one with a Creative Commons licence, and recognises that licence conditions apply.
